analysis.one_liner: Cuts income, corporate, capital gains, and payroll taxes and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill had zero cosponsors, was never taken up by the Ways and Means Committee, and died without a hearing or vote when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten large parts of the tax code: a flat 20% rate on individual income up to $1 million and 30% above that, a 20% corporate rate (down from 35%), a 15% cap on capital gains taxes, a permanent 5% tax on corporations bringing foreign profits home, permanent 100% expensing of business equipment, half the Social Security and Medicare payroll tax, and full repeal of the estate and gift taxes. It was referred to the tax-writing committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and high-income households gain the most: the 30% top rate is well below the existing top rate, capital gains and corporate rates fall sharply, foreign profits come home at 5%, equipment can be written off instantly, and the estate tax on very large inheritances disappears. Employees and self-employed people would see a small raise in take-home pay from the halved payroll tax.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the corporate rate from 35% to a single 20% rate on all corporate income.
Caps the tax on capital gains — profits from selling investments — at 15%, a rate only the wealthiest investors currently pay near.
Sets a permanent 5% effective tax on U.S. corporations' foreign earnings brought back to the United States, covering both current and accumulated offshore profits.
Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely for deaths and gifts after enactment.
Halves the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare, raising take-home pay for workers and cutting the self-employment tax from 12.4% plus 2.9% to roughly 6.2% plus 1.45%.
Makes permanent a 100% bonus depreciation allowance, letting businesses deduct the full cost of equipment immediately.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government loses revenue from every major source — income, corporate, capital gains, payroll, and estate taxes — which must be made up through borrowing or cuts elsewhere. Halving payroll tax collections directly starves the Social Security and Medicare trust funds that current retirees and future beneficiaries depend on.

drawbacks.text: Halving FICA and SECA rates would cut Social Security and Medicare funding roughly in half; unlike the income tax, those programs are financed by the payroll tax, and the bill provides no replacement funding.

The bill lowers rates on income from wealth — capital gains capped at 15%, estate tax repealed, corporate profits taxed at 20% — while the gains to wage earners are limited to the payroll tax cut, shifting the tax burden away from the wealthiest households.

The combination of a 20% corporate rate, 100% expensing, permanent 5% repatriation, and repeal of the estate tax would reduce federal revenue substantially, implying larger deficits or future spending cuts.

The 20% individual rate on income up to $1 million replaces the existing progressive brackets, cutting taxes most for high earners while offering wage earners only the temporary cushion of a halved payroll tax that undermines the benefits it funds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Workers would get a genuine short-term raise from the halved payroll tax, but that cut comes directly out of the funding for Social Security and Medicare — the programs the tax exists to pay for — with no alternative revenue offered. The other provisions concentrate their benefits on corporations, investors, and large estates. Weighed honestly, the bill trades a modest, self-defeating benefit for workers against large, permanent tax reductions for concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams introduced the Jump Start America Act of 2017 on April 6, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never left committee and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, current Social Security and Medicare funding remained intact and corporations and wealthy households forgo the rate cuts and estate tax repeal it would have given them. Working people and beneficiaries are better off than under the bill as written.

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: The House committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party, so its support never took a partisan shape in the record.

industries.note: The bill cuts the corporate rate from 35% to 20%, taxes repatriated foreign profits at 5%, and allows immediate full expensing of equipment — a large, permanent revenue transfer financed by borrowing. The general public bears the cost of the lost revenue while shareholders gain.

A 30% top rate replaces the existing 39.6% top bracket, capital gains are capped at 15%, and the estate tax is repealed outright — the tax that applies only to the largest inheritances. These are direct cuts to taxes on wealth.

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals and small business owners
industries.note: The self-employment tax is roughly halved, immediately boosting net income for sole proprietors, though the same cut drains the Social Security and Medicare accounts they will draw on later.
Both sides of the payroll tax are halved, which raises take-home pay now but removes the dedicated funding stream for Social Security and Medicare benefits workers and retirees are counting on.
